question: Azof Brigade fascists are touring Europe to raise funds and recruit Ukrainian ‘members and volunteers’ who left for other countries, media reports say. Four members of this Nazi military unit, which forms part of the Ukrainian armed forces have scheduled events in nine European cities in Poland, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Czechia and Lithuania, over less than 15 days.

The governments of the countries they are visiting have obviously either approved or are tolerating this tour. While the EU has added to its sanction list Russian neo-Nazi armed groups that have been incorporated into the Russian army in the past two years, such as ‘Rusich’, Ukrainian Nazis are being treated quite differently, with tolerance and even overt support being shown to them.

In addition to the support, funding and equipment the EU has been providing to Ukraine’s Nazi military units, we are also witnessing unacceptable tributes being paid to Nazi collaborators in other EU Member States too, such as Estonia, where just a few days ago the Government showed tolerance towards a demonstration by a few dozen people dressed in Nazi Wehrmacht uniform. In view of this: 1.

What is the Commission’s view of the visits paid by Azof Brigade Nazis to EU Member States, with the tolerance at the very least, if not the support of the governments of the respective Member States?
What is the Commission’s view of the unacceptable events at which tributes have been paid to Nazi collaborators in a number of countries such as Estonia in this case?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.11.2024) The Commission is not aware of visits mentioned by the Honourable Members and cannot comment on matters which appear to fall under national competence.

The Commission would like to recall that it condemns any form of violence and hatred, including manifestations of racism, antisemitism, xenophobia and other forms of intolerance which are incompatible with the EU values. Glorifying Nazism and trivializing the Holocaust have no place in European democracy. The Framework Decision on combating racism and xenophobia1 obliges EU Member States to criminalise hate speech2.

It is for the national authorities to establish whether the national criminal law provisions implementing the Framework Decision apply in specific circumstances, taking into account the context and the situation of each case.
1 Council Framework Decision 2008/913/JHA of 28 November 2008 on combating certain forms and

expressions of racism and xenophobia by means of criminal law, L 328/55. 2 Hate speech is defined in the Framework Decision as public incitement to violence or hatred directed against a group of persons or a member of such a group defined by reference to race, colour, religion, descent or national or ethnic origin.
